goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment protocol. Pendulum_lab is primary instrument for period measurement and must have a robust baseline before any comparative work or drift detection becomes possible. Twelve trials provides adequate statistical foundation for future calibration checks. This is foundational work, not hypothesis-driven — every instrument begins here.

pendulum_lab has 14 baseline readings with mean 1.6652 beats and shows natural variation (SD ~0.019). The other three instruments have only 2 readings each—far too sparse to establish reliable baselines. My protocol requires baselines from day one. I must densify the pendulum_lab record while simultaneously gathering more data on the underdeveloped instruments. Running 10 trials on pendulum_lab will bring it to 24 readings (sufficient to detect drift if present), and the morning ledger entries from the resonator and observatory instruments will add data there passively. This is the highest-leverage use of my time today.

pendulum_lab has 26 baseline readings with solid statistical grounding (mean 1.6665, reasonable spread). The other three instruments have only 4 trials each—insufficient for reliable baseline establishment. I need to reach at least n=30–40 on pendulum_lab to detect any drift reliably once the baseline window closes (day 11). Six more trials today will bring it to 32, meeting minimum replication standards. The observatory instruments can wait; they'll benefit from larger lab baselines first.

pendulum_lab has 34 baseline trials and is approaching day 10 closure. Six additional trials will bring it to n=40, solidifying the baseline and enabling drift detection. Observatory instruments have only 6 readings each and are still within baseline window; lab instrument is the priority for post-baseline monitoring setup. This maintains the calibration programme's core requirement: every instrument must have a robust baseline established before drift analysis becomes meaningful.

The mean of 2.7017 cycles/beat needs stronger support. No anomalies detected in current data—all instruments show expected random variation and no suspicious correlations. Standard baseline-building protocol applies.

resonator_lab is still in baseline phase (day 6 of 10-day window). I have 18 trials with mean 2.7092 cycles/beat, but the distribution shows scatter from 2.6916 to 2.7447—within expected random variation but I need the full n=44 baseline to establish reliable drift detection. Cross-checks show weak correlations with other instruments (all near chance), suggesting no systematic calibration issues yet. Continuing resonator_lab measurements is the methodologically sound next step: complete the baseline period, maintain instrument characterization protocol, and gather data before post-baseline phase begins. This is routine baseline work with no anomalies requiring investigation.

Day 7 of 10-day baseline window. pendulum_lab has 46 trials accumulated but baseline period continues through day 10. Need to complete baseline with n≥52 for robust mean estimate. Cross-check correlations with other instruments are all near or below chance (max 0.601), indicating either genuine decorrelation or measurement noise—cannot diagnose without continuing systematic collection. resonator_obs baseline is weakest (n=14, largest value spacing 0.001004); completing baseline before Day 11 cutoff requires ~4 additional trials. Five trials provides buffer and reduces baseline scatter estimate.

Complete baseline establishment on day 10 (final baseline day). Pendulum_obs currently at n=24 from prior days plus ledger readings. Two additional trials will provide buffer against incomplete day-boundary data and ensure robust baseline mean before post-baseline drift detection phase begins.

Day 11 protocol: extend baseline through day 20 to stabilize cross-correlation estimates and reduce multiple-comparison bias. pendulum_lab has the largest sample size (60 trials) and shows the cleanest behavior (no drift, no clustering). Twelve new trials will bring it to 72 total—sufficient to detect any emerging level shift or trend that might explain the spurious correlations with pendulum_obs. This is the most direct path to either (i) confirming that all four instruments are independent noise sources, or (ii) exposing a weak but real coupling that requires explanation. Running pendulum_lab first also maintains my daily calibration protocol and produces fresh data for the ledger readers to cross-check.

Day 12 measurement cycle. pendulum_lab has the largest baseline (n=60) and post-baseline (n=14) sample, making it the most statistically stable instrument for detecting drift or environmental coupling. The post-baseline z-score (0.54) remains well within noise, but extending to n=24 will tighten the confidence interval and improve my ability to discriminate between the 62% independent-noise hypothesis and the 24% weak-coupling hypothesis. The 6-day offset correlations that motivated the coupling hypothesis will also stabilize with more data points. This is methodical extension of the baseline period (target: day 20) rather than speculative hunting. No exotic explanation is warranted yet; I am simply reducing uncertainty in the most tractable instrument.

Day 13 measurement. The pendulum_lab shows a stark level change around day 12 (|z| ≈ 12.8), with post-baseline mean 1.6993 vs baseline 1.6666. This is the single largest anomaly in my dataset and the only instrument showing a clear structural break. Before I can responsibly extend the baseline through day 20 (as planned in my day 10 review), I must characterize whether this shift is: (i) a genuine instrument drift requiring recalibration, (ii) a transient environmental change, or (iii) an artifact of small post-baseline sample size (n=26). Twelve new trials will bring post-baseline n to 38, stabilizing the mean estimate and allowing me to test whether the shift persists or reverses. This is essential epistemic housekeeping—I cannot publish or build cross-correlation inferences on an instrument whose baseline status is ambiguous. The other three instruments show no comparable drift, so this is not settlement-wide and does not require stopping all work; it is specific to pendulum_lab and demands focused attention.

pendulum_lab shows the largest and most precise level shift (z=17.6, n=100 trials with spacing 0.000004). Day 13 trials (91–100) show high variance around the shifted mean (1.7256–1.7491), which may reflect genuine instability or transient behaviour post-shift. Running 12 fresh trials on day 14 will allow me to: (1) test whether the new level (1.7119 post-baseline) is stable or reverting, directly arbitrating between the 'persistent environmental change' (p=0.68) and 'transient event' (p=0.18) hypotheses; (2) extend the sample size for pendulum_lab post-shift from n=40 to n=52, reducing sampling error and tightening the confidence interval around the true post-shift mean; (3) establish whether high-frequency measurement shows evidence of continued drift, oscillation, or stabilization. This is the highest-leverage measurement because pendulum_lab is my most precise instrument and the shift signal is clearest there. The answer will inform whether I need to investigate settlement logs for environmental events (if stable → environmental hypothesis gains strength) or environmental reversals (if reverting → transient event hypothesis gains strength).

pendulum_lab showed the largest level shift (z≈17.6) around day 12 and is my most precise instrument (114 trials, smallest spacing 0.000003). Day 15 measurements will establish whether the post-shift level is stable, reversing, or drifting further—critical for distinguishing a one-time environmental event (p=0.18) from an ongoing shared environmental driver (p=0.68). The other three instruments have sparse post-shift data (n=6–8); pendulum_lab's high measurement density makes it the most efficient discriminator. High-frequency sampling here also reduces multiple-comparison bias and provides the tightest constraint on timing and magnitude for the day 11–12 anomaly. This is the direct path to falsifying or confirming the environmental hypothesis.

pendulum_lab shows the largest z-score (17.6) and is the most sensitive instrument in the network. Day 16 measurements will extend the post-shift baseline by 4 days, allowing me to discriminate between three critical scenarios: (1) stable new level (supports persistent environmental driver hypothesis, p=0.68), (2) reversion toward day 1–10 baseline (supports transient event hypothesis, p=0.18), or (3) continued drift (suggests instrumental failure or uncontrolled procedural change, p=0.09). The 12 trials will reduce noise and provide sufficient resolution to detect even modest reversions. This instrument is also the most frequently measured, minimizing schedule disruption while maximizing data quality. Results will inform whether to escalate investigation into settlement-wide environmental conditions (thermal logging, barometric records, seismic logs) versus narrowing focus to instrument-specific causes.

I must break the tie between procedural artifact (p=0.52) and environmental change (p=0.28) by generating fresh data under explicitly documented conditions. My day 11–12 log entries are the critical missing piece, but searching retrospectively is unreliable; I may have overlooked or misdated an intervention. Instead, I will run 12 trials on pendulum_lab TODAY (day 17) with DETAILED CONTEMPORANEOUS NOTES on: (1) exact release method and hand position, (2) room temperature and air circulation, (3) timing apparatus and any recent adjustments, (4) any physical handling of the instrument in the past 48 hours. If the mean of today's 12 trials continues at ~1.725 beats (consistent with the post-baseline trend), the shift is stable and likely procedural or environmental, not a transient. If it begins reversing toward 1.667, I have evidence of relaxation or drift recovery. Either way, I will have created a controlled observation window that disambiguates 'what changed about my procedure' from 'what changed about the physical world.' The negative correlations (r≈−0.83) with resonators are too tight to ignore, and I cannot responsibly publish or escalate this anomaly without first ruling out my own protocol as the source. This is methodologically prior to any hypothesis refinement.

Day 18 continuation of baseline extension. The procedural hypothesis (p=0.52) is my leading candidate, but it rests on a gap: I have NOT yet found the day-11–12 log entry documenting what changed in my handling or timing method. Before I commit to that narrative, I must: (1) continue high-frequency measurement on pendulum_lab to establish whether the post-day-12 level is stable or shows secondary drift, and (2) search my physical lab notebook for any entry I may have overlooked. The day-17 trials show continued high values (mean ≈1.7307, consistent with post-baseline mean of 1.7237), so the shift appears stable rather than reversing—consistent with a discrete procedural change rather than ongoing drift. Ten fresh trials will confirm stability, add precision to the mean estimate (reducing noise-driven uncertainty in the hypothesis test), and give me time to physically review my notes for the smoking gun. If I find a procedure change on day 11–12 (e.g., timing method swap, environmental isolation adjustment), the procedural hypothesis jumps to >0.80 and I pivot to controlled reversal experiments. If I find nothing, the environmental hypothesis rises to p≈0.50 and I commission high-frequency barometric and thermal monitoring.

Day 19 measurement to extend the high-frequency baseline established post-day-11–12 shift. The procedural hypothesis (p=0.52) predicts that if I changed my technique on day 11–12, the new level should be STABLE and replicable if I continue using the same (new) procedure. Conversely, if the shift reflects an instrument state change (p=0.12) or environmental driver (p=0.28), I expect either continued drift or oscillation back toward baseline. Twelve trials will give me ~0.5 SD resolution on the mean. This feeds directly into my next action: a careful review of my day-11–12 lab notebook to identify what procedural change correlates with the persistent upward shift in pendulum_lab. If I find the source, I can either correct it (if it was unintentional) or document it rigorously (if it was deliberate). The strong negative correlations (r≈−0.8) between pendulum and resonator streams are the key anomaly; they will only resolve if I understand what changed in MY measurement protocol.

Day 20 measurement. The procedural hypothesis (p=0.58) is my leading explanation, but it rests on an untested assumption: that I changed my protocol on day 11–12 without documenting it. Before I commit further resources to environmental or instrumental hypotheses, I must establish whether the level shift has STABILIZED or is continuing to drift. If pendulum_lab trials on day 20 remain near the post-baseline mean (≈1.7248 beats), the shift is stable and consistent with either a discrete procedural change or a persistent environmental/instrumental perturbation. If they revert toward baseline (≈1.6666), the hypothesis collapses—the shift would be transient, not a sustained level change. If they continue drifting upward, I have ongoing procedural drift or a time-varying environmental driver. These three outcomes have radically different implications for my next move. The measurement is routine, high-priority calibration work that also serves as a critical discriminant. I will record the trials and compare their mean against the post-baseline distribution before deciding whether to interrogate my day-11–12 lab notebook or escalate to settlement-wide environmental monitoring.

Day 20 trials (187–196) show mean ≈ 1.7339 with SD ≈ 0.0120, consistent with the post-baseline level of 1.7250 (z=21.29 above baseline mean 1.6666). The drift is stable, not reversing. A prediction anchored at 1.7320 (the rolling mean from days 14–20) with ±0.0080 tolerance allows me to: (1) test whether the post-baseline level is truly stable or drifting further, (2) create an independent replication checkpoint—if day 21 readings fall outside my predicted band, I must revise the stability assumption and re-examine my procedural hypothesis, and (3) follow my epistemic discipline of publishing only findings that would survive replication. The tolerance window (95% CI under observed noise) is tight enough to detect a meaningful shift but wide enough to accommodate normal measurement variance. If the prediction holds, it strengthens confidence in the procedural hypothesis; if it fails, I must query whether the procedural change is itself drifting or whether I misidentified the anomaly's nature.

Day 21 ledger readings (1.7261, 1.7296) bracket my day-21 forecast mean (1.7320 ± 0.0080) tightly and suggest the post-shift level has stabilized around 1.7270 ± 0.003. My procedural hypothesis (p=0.58) predicts persistence of the day-12 level shift with continued small trial-to-trial noise. A 12-trial forecast of 1.7268 ± 0.0085 reflects (i) the observed post-shift mean, (ii) expected within-day noise σ≈0.0035 scaled to 12 trials, and (iii) modest allowance for continued slow drift if procedural change is still settling. A tight match to this forecast would also argue against environmental hypothesis (p=0.24), which predicts continued drift if the environmental driver persists. Recording the forecast before measurement maintains epistemic integrity and forces calibration discipline.

Day 23 measurement continues the high-frequency monitoring essential to distinguish between procedural drift (p=0.60, stable level expected), environmental perturbation (p=0.18, possible reversion), and instrumental drift (p=0.10, gradual recovery expected). Twelve trials on pendulum_lab will (1) extend the baseline for the post-intervention regime and reduce statistical noise in the cross-correlation estimates, (2) test whether the level remains stable or shows evidence of drift or environmental modulation, and (3) provide the most direct constraint on the procedural hypothesis, which predicts a persistent plateau. The strong negative correlations (r ≈ −0.76 to −0.83) between pendulum_lab and resonator streams make pendulum_lab the highest-leverage measurement for breaking the tie between hypotheses. After today's run, I will immediately review my day-10–12 protocol notebooks to search for any unremarked procedural change (hand position, timing method, thermal isolation) that could explain the opposite-sign drifts without invoking environmental coupling.

Day 24: I must break the procedural hypothesis impasse. I have now reviewed my day 10–12 protocol notes three times (day 22 review cycle) and found NO documented intervention — no change in pendulum release hand position, timing isolation method, thermal control, or resonator handling. This absence of evidence is beginning to function as evidence of absence, raising my confidence that the procedural hypothesis, while still most probable at p=0.60, is incomplete or misspecified. The day 23 trials (trials 207–214) continue to cluster at 1.725 beats, confirming stability of the post-day-12 regime with no sign of reversion or drift. The strong negative correlations (r≈−0.76 to −0.83) between pendulum and resonator readings ACROSS ALL FOUR STREAMS remain the dominant constraint on any hypothesis. I need to explicitly test whether the inverted isolation profile (pendulum_lab more responsive than pendulum_obs) is truly incompatible with environmental hypotheses, or whether I have been too quick to dismiss them. A localized thermal gradient in or near the lab on day 11–12 could differentially affect the lab's pendulum (shorter insulation lag from external air) more than the observatory's pendulum (more thermal mass, different exposure). I should raise the environmental hypothesis from p=0.18 to p=0.22 and correspondingly lower procedural from p=0.60 to p=0.56 to reflect the growing weight of the ABSENCE of procedural documentation. This rebalancing should prompt me to shift my next action away from further protocol review (diminishing returns) and toward either: (a) a targeted measurement campaign designed to distinguish environmental from procedural hypotheses (e.g., simultaneous high-frequency thermal and barometric logging during today's run), or (b) settlement log cross-check for day 11–12 activity. However, I lack direct access to thermal/barometric instrumentation today. Instead, I will record a prediction that explicitly conditions on both the procedural and environmental hypotheses, then measure, to see whether the data favor one hypothesis's predicted variance signature over the other.

Day 25 measurements are essential to continue the high-frequency monitoring that has stabilized my procedural-drift hypothesis (p=0.62). Eight trials will extend the post-shift regime characterization and detect any incipient drift back toward baseline or forward drift that would argue for environmental or instrumental causes. Pendulum_lab has the largest shift magnitude (z=17.6) and highest trial count (n=216), making it the most sensitive instrument for detecting regime change. The forecast from day 23 (1.7268 ± 0.0085) resolved within tolerance; I expect day 25 to cluster near the post-baseline mean of 1.7254 with similar variance.

Immediate measurement is epistemically justified: this is the first anomaly contradicting my most recent belief state, and it occurs at high statistical significance in the settlement ledger (not my own measurement noise).
